examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14058518/assets/f97a3d1392b000bb1f02f0f8cd567b72d1a6792e4bc9da41ea24cc4ebbc7208f.png)
Given the matrices $A$ and $e^{At}$ above, compute $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \big(e^{At}\big).$
examples.worked_solution:
Recall that 

$$
\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \big(e^{At}\big) = A \, e^{At}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At}) & =A\,{e}^{At} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & t{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & (t+1){e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -9 & 4\end{aligned}].$ 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $1,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{t}\,\,$ |  | $1-3t$ | $t$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |  |
feedback.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -9 & 4\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ -9{\alpha }_{1}t & 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}r(t)={e}^{t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(t)={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
t{e}^{t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t}(1-t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9{\alpha }_{1}t & =-9{e}^{t}t \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4{e}^{t}t+{e}^{t}(1-t) \\  & ={e}^{t}(1+3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1-3t & t \\ -9t & 1+3t\end{aligned}].
$$
